caption: Field and venue of the papers at each stage of the corpus. OpenAlex is an open index of scholarly works that supplies each paper's journal, publisher, citation counts and topic labels. The pool is every 2022 candidate article from OpenAlex (n = 14,223): research articles with an abstract and at least 15 references, from publishers with a full-text route, in two rings: the core ring is the 8 OpenAlex topics of the study's principal investigator (the convenor: seismology, seismic waves and imaging, earthquakes, seismic sensors, cryosphere, high-pressure geophysics), the broad ring 8 Earth-science subfields. Round 1 preselected 600: half per ring, equal numbers from each quintile of cnp (OpenAlex citation normalized percentile, a paper's citation rank among works of the same OpenAlex subfield, year and type, 0 to 1) and, within a quintile, subfields taken in turn. The core ring is 19% of the pool and half of round 1, so the convenor's topics are over-represented by design. Eligible papers passed an abstract screen by two independent language-model screeners (a third settled disagreements) that drops off-topic papers, reviews and comments or replies; full text means a PDF was retrieved; coded means a Claude model (claude-opus-5-5, codebook 1.5.0) read the full text and returned a coding, the paper's research workflow written as a graph of modes of inquiry defined in the codebook, that passes the schema check of tools/check_coding.py (schema fields and values, steps numbered in order, each step with a page and a quote of at most 25 words) (round 1: 525 eligible, 379 full text, 233 coded, so 146 papers with full text have no valid coding yet; the check says nothing about whether a coding is right). Round 2 drew 277 open-access papers from the rest of the pool, at most 4 per journal (222 eligible, 202 full text, coding batch not yet returned). (a) Share of papers by OpenAlex subfield, the subfield of the paper's leading topic as assigned by OpenAlex's classifier (a machine label, not an author keyword); the 6 subfields with the largest share at any stage are coloured, the rest grey; numbers in segments are percentages. OpenAlex files topics, not papers, under subfields, so a subfield name can mislead: where one leading topic holds at least 60% of a subfield's coded papers, the label gives it. Atmospheric Science: 81 of 125 round-1 preselected papers have the leading topic Cryospheric studies and observations; Artificial Intelligence: 64 of 64 round-1 preselected papers have the leading topic Seismology and Earthquake Studies; Ocean Engineering: 19 of 19 round-1 preselected papers have the leading topic Geophysics and Sensor Technology; Space and Planetary Science: 4 of 4 round-1 preselected papers have the leading topic Archaeological Research and Protection. Of the 17 coded papers in the subfield Artificial Intelligence, 13 use machine-learning terms somewhere in their coding and 6 build a new capability described in such terms; they are seismology papers, many of them machine-learning seismology. (b) Share by journal family, the publisher group read from the DOI prefix, then the publisher name: AGU, American Geophysical Union journals (published by Wiley, counted apart from other Wiley journals); Copernicus (mostly EGU), journals published by Copernicus (DOI prefix 10.5194), nearly all of the European Geosciences Union, plus European Journal of Mineralogy and Scientific Drilling; Nature portfolio, Nature-branded journals, Scientific Reports and Communications Earth & Environment; Springer Nature (other), the rest of Springer Nature; SSA, Seismological Society of America; Oxford, Oxford University Press (Geophysical Journal International). Right: effective number of journals, 1/HHI where the Herfindahl index HHI is the sum of squared journal shares (the number of equally sized journals giving the same concentration), and distinct journals. (c) The 12 journals with the most coded papers (round 1; coded count in brackets): share of papers in the pool (grey, n = 14,223), among eligible papers (orange, n = 525) and among coded papers (green, n = 233), log axis. The Cryosphere holds 1.7% of the pool, 6.3% of eligible and 14.2% of coded papers. (d) Coverage by journal family among round 1 eligible papers: the rate of a step in the family minus the rate in all other families, in percentage points, for full text retrieved (hollow) and coded (filled), with 95% percentile bootstrap intervals (2000 resamples over papers); 0 means the family reaches the step as often as the rest; families with fewer than 10 eligible papers are pooled. Right: share of the family's eligible papers that are coded, and their number. How strongly a grouping decides coverage is given by Cramér's V, the association between two categorical variables (here the grouping and whether a paper reached the step), bias-corrected (Bergsma 2013) so that small samples with many categories are not inflated; 0 = independent, 1 = the grouping decides coverage; it measures association, not cause. The intervals are percentile intervals of the resampled V, which is biased upward under resampling, so read them as spread, not as bias-corrected intervals: family against full text 0.79 [0.74, 0.83], against coded 0.73 [0.69, 0.78], against coded among papers with full text 0.86 [0.81, 0.91]; subfield against full text 0.34 [0.28, 0.44], against coded 0.26 [0.19, 0.36], against coded among papers with full text 0.12 [0.00, 0.28]. Statistics from tools/roadmap/g20_topics_journals.py (descriptive; permutation tests and Benjamini-Hochberg q, the false-discovery-rate adjusted p value, in topics_journals.json); journal shares in (c) recounted from the same records. Source: OpenAlex (retrieved October 2026), round manifests, download queue and model codings; figure date 2026-10-27.
